1F (Linear Algebra)

Words: 335 Articles: 6
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

i

Words: 175 Articles: 1
1F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 175
i OurBigBook.com
The Steinitz exchange lemma says that if w1​,…,wm​ span a vector space and v1​,…,vr​ are linearly independent, then r≤m, and after reordering the wj​, the family v1​,…,vr​,wr+1​,…,wm​ still spans. Here is a proof. Suppose the first k−1 replacements have been made. Express vk​ in that spanning family. Some coefficient of a remaining wj​ must be nonzero, since otherwise vk​ belongs to the span of v1​,…,vk−1​, contrary to linear independence. Solve for that wj​ and replace it by vk​; this preserves spanning. If r>m, the first m replacements leave a spanning family v1​,…,vm​, contradicting linear independence of the first m+1 vectors. This proves both assertions.
Now suppose S is linearly independent and spans Rn. Express each member of the standard basis using finitely many members of S, and let S0​ be the finite union of those members. Then S0​ spans. No element of S∖S0​ can exist, since it would be a linear combination of S0​ and violate linear independence. Thus S is finite. Applying the Steinitz exchange lemma in both directions to S and the standard basis gives ∣S∣≤n and n≤∣S∣. Hence ∣S∣=n​.

ii

Words: 41 Articles: 1
1F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 41
ii OurBigBook.com
If S is linearly independent and has n elements, apply the Steinitz exchange lemma with S as the independent family and the standard basis as the spanning family. All n members of the standard basis are replaced, leaving S itself spanning. Thus spanS=Rn​, so S is a basis.

iii

Words: 119 Articles: 1
1F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 119
iii OurBigBook.com
If S spans and has n elements but is linearly dependent, a nontrivial linear combination equal to zero lets us remove one member without changing the span. This produces n−1 spanning vectors, whereas the standard basis contains n linearly independent vectors, contradicting the Steinitz exchange lemma. Therefore S is linearly independent​. Together the three deductions establish that any two of the three properties imply the third. For n=0, the only independent or zero-element family is the empty basis, and the same conclusions hold.
Relative to the given basis e1​,e2​, the proposed vectors are the columns of
M=(λ1​1λ​),detM=λ2−1.
(1)
The determinant is nonzero exactly when the columns form a basis. Thus λ=±1​. At λ=1 the vectors coincide, and at λ=−1 they are negatives of one another.

2A (Complex Analysis or Complex Methods)

Words: 100 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 100
2A OurBigBook.com
For complex differentiability at a point, the derivative must have the same value along real and imaginary increments. Along real increments it equals ux​+ivx​, while along imaginary increments it equals (uy​+ivy​)/i=vy​−iuy​. Equating real and imaginary parts gives the Cauchy-Riemann equations
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​​.
(2)
For the given real part,
ux​=(x2+y2)2y2−x2​,uy​=(x2+y2)2−2xy​.
(3)
Integrating the Cauchy-Riemann equations gives a harmonic conjugate
v(x,y)=−x2+y2y​+C,F(z)=z1​+iC,D=C∖{0}​,C∈R.
(4)
This open set is open and connected; F is holomorphic there with derivative −z−2. The origin must be excluded because the real part is undefined there. On this connected open set, any other harmonic conjugate differs by a real constant: the Cauchy-Riemann equations make both partial derivatives of the difference zero.

3G (Geometry)

Words: 181 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 181
3G OurBigBook.com
In the curvature −1 normalization, the hyperbolic triangle area is its angle defect:
area(T)=π−α−β−γ​.
(5)
Join one vertex of a convex geodesic polygon to its nonadjacent vertices. This gives n−2 hyperbolic triangles with disjoint interiors. Their angles at every polygon vertex sum to that vertex's interior angle. Adding the hyperbolic triangle areas therefore gives the hyperbolic polygon area
A=(n−2)π−j=1∑n​αj​​.
(6)
For a regular hyperbolic polygon with prescribed area, place n equally spaced vertices on a hyperbolic circle of radius R>0 and join consecutive vertices by geodesics. Rotations through 2π/n and reflections in radial lines show that this is a convex regular polygon. The triangle from its centre to a vertex and the midpoint of an adjacent side is right angled, with angles π/n, α(R)/2, and π/2, and hypotenuse R. The angle form of the hyperbolic law of cosines gives
coshR=cot(π/n)cot(α(R)/2),α(R)=2arctan(coshRcot(π/n)​).
(7)
Consequently A(R)=(n−2)π−nα(R) is continuous and strictly increasing. As R↓0, α(R)→π−2π/n, so A(R)→0; as R→∞, α(R)→0, so A(R)→(n−2)π. The intermediate value theorem proves existence for every permitted A. Indeed the required radius is
R=arcosh[tan(((n−2)π−A)/(2n))cot(π/n)​]​.
(8)
The argument also proves uniqueness of the radius in this construction; neither endpoint area is attained by a nondegenerate finite-radius polygon.

4D (Variational Principles)

Words: 124 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 124
4D OurBigBook.com
Take a smooth variation uε​=u+εϕ with ϕ=0 on the boundary. Assume enough differentiability for the following operations, for example a smooth bounded open set, u∈C2, and a twice continuously differentiable integrand. Differentiation under the integral gives
dεdI[uε​]​​0​=∫D​(Lu​ϕ+Lux​​ϕx​+Luy​​ϕy​)dxdy.
(9)
By integration by parts, the boundary term vanishes and the first variation is
∫D​(Lu​−∂x​Lux​​−∂y​Luy​​)ϕdxdy.
(10)
Stationarity for every such variation, including every compactly supported smooth one, and the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations give the Euler-Lagrange equation
Lu​−∂x​Lux​​−∂y​Luy​​=0​.
(11)
For the quadratic integrand, Lu​=2k2u, Lux​​=2ux​, and Luy​​=2uy​. Thus
uxx​+uyy​=k2u​
(12)
with the prescribed Dirichlet boundary condition. For real k, a stationary function is also the unique minimizer, if it exists: for any nonzero admissible ϕ, the linear term vanishes and I[u+ϕ]−I[u]=∫D​(∣∇ϕ∣2+k2ϕ2)>0. This last positivity uses the zero boundary values; it also holds at k=0.

i OurBigBook.com
The divergence and scalar vorticity are
∇⋅u=∂x​(2xy)+∂y​(x2+y2)=4y,∂x​uy​−∂y​ux​=2x−2x=0.
(13)
Thus the flow is irrotational but not incompressible on the plane. A velocity potential satisfying u=∇ϕ is
ϕ=x2y+3y3​+C​.
(14)
Indeed its two partial derivatives are the two velocity components. A usual two-dimensional stream function would satisfy ux​=ψy​, uy​=−ψx​ and hence have identically zero divergence. No such stream function exists on an open region where this divergence is not identically zero; the line y=0 is not a two-dimensional flow domain.

ii

Words: 80 Articles: 1
5D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 80
ii OurBigBook.com
Here both the divergence and vorticity vanish:
∂x​(−2y)+∂y​(−2x)=0,∂x​(−2x)−∂y​(−2y)=−2+2=0.
(15)
The flow is incompressible and irrotational. With u=∇ϕ and (ux​,uy​)=(ψy​,−ψx​),
ϕ=−2xy+C,ψ=x2−y2+C′​.
(16)
The streamlines are the level sets x2−y2=constant. To determine the arrows, put r=x+y and s=x−y. A particle satisfies r˙=−2r, s˙=2s. Thus the separatrix y=x approaches the stagnation point at the origin, whereas y=−x leaves it; the other streamlines are hyperbolas following those asymptotes. The origin itself is a stationary particle.

6C (Numerical Analysis)

Words: 164 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 164
6C OurBigBook.com
The Lagrange cardinal polynomials are
ℓi​(x)=∏0≤j≤nj=i​​xi​−xj​x−xj​​,ℓi​(xj​)=δij​.
(17)
Thus the Lagrange interpolation polynomial is
p(x)=i=0∑n​fi​ℓi​(x)​.
(18)
It has degree at most n and takes the required values. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two such polynomials has n+1 distinct roots and degree at most n, so is zero. The source's phrase “degree n” must allow a smaller degree, for example when f is constant.
Define the divided difference recursively by f[xi​]=fi​ and
f[x0​,…,xn​]=xn​−x0​f[x1​,…,xn​]−f[x0​,…,xn−1​]​.
(19)
Induction on this recursion, or comparison of the leading coefficient in the Newton interpolation polynomial, gives
f[x0​,…,xn​]=i=0∑n​∏j=i​(xi​−xj​)fi​​​.
(20)
For completeness the induction works term by term: an interior term gets the coefficient (1/(xi​−xn​)−1/(xi​−x0​))/(xn​−x0​)=1/((xi​−xn​)(xi​−x0​)), multiplying the product over the other interior nodes; the two endpoint terms give the same formula. This is also the leading coefficient of p directly from the cardinal formula, so p(n)=n!f[x0​,…,xn​].
The function f−p∈Cn[x0​,xn​] has n+1 distinct zeros. Repeated application of Rolle theorem gives ξ∈(x0​,xn​) with (f−p)(n)(ξ)=0 when n≥1. Hence
f[x0​,…,xn​]=n!f(n)(ξ)​​.
(21)
For n=0, this is simply f[x0​]=f(x0​) and we take ξ=x0​.

7H (Statistics)

Words: 243 Articles: 4
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 120 Articles: 1
7H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
a OurBigBook.com
The Rao-Blackwell theorem applies to an estimator Y with finite second moment and a sufficient statistic T. The conditional estimator Y∗=Eθ​[Y∣T] can be chosen as a function of the observed T that does not depend on the unknown parameter: this uses the parameter-independent conditional data distribution in the definition of sufficient statistic. The tower property of conditional expectation gives Eθ​Y∗=Eθ​Y, so their bias agrees. The law of total variance gives
Varθ​Y=Varθ​Y∗+Eθ​Varθ​(Y∣T).
(22)
For any target a(θ) it follows that
Eθ​[(Y∗−a(θ))2]≤Eθ​[(Y−a(θ))2]​.
(23)
Equality holds exactly when Y=Y∗ almost surely under that parameter value. This proves variance reduction and reduction of mean squared error, whether or not the original estimator is an unbiased estimator. More generally, conditional Jensen inequality proves the corresponding inequality for any convex loss in the estimate, whenever the expectations exist.

Since P(X1​=0)=e−λ, the indicator Y is an unbiased estimator of θ. The joint probability mass function is
pλ​(x1​,…,xn​)=e−nλ∏i​xi​!λ∑i​xi​​.
(24)
The Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem therefore makes T=∑i​Xi​ a sufficient statistic. More explicitly, conditioning on T=t gives a multinomial distribution with t trials and cell probabilities 1/n, so X1​∣T=t has the binomial distribution Bin(t,1/n). Consequently conditioning by the Rao-Blackwell theorem gives
E[Y∣T]=(1−n1​)T​.
(25)
For n=1, interpret the value at T=0 as 1 and at T>0 as 0; thus the same expression uses 00=1 in this probability convention. For λ=0 all observations and T are zero almost surely. For n>1 and λ>0, the reduction in variance is strict: given T=1, the event X1​=0 still has a nondegenerate conditional probability. Directly, using the probability generating function of T∼Poisson(nλ), the new variance is e−2λ(eλ/n−1).

8H OurBigBook.com
Introduce nonnegative slack variables s1​,s2​ and use the origin as the initial feasible simplex basis:
s1​=10−x1​−x2​−2x3​,s2​=15−2x1​−x2​−3x3​,z=x1​+2x2​+x3​.
(26)
In the simplex method, let x2​ enter. The ratio test is min(10,15)=10, so s1​ leaves. Solving the first constraint for x2​ yields the dictionary
x2​=10−x1​−2x3​−s1​,s2​=5−x1​−x3​+s1​,z=20−x1​−3x3​−2s1​.
(27)
All nonbasic variables are nonnegative and have negative reduced objective coefficients. Setting them to zero is feasible and optimal:
(x1​,x2​,x3​)=(0,10,0),zmax​=20​.
(28)
Subtracting Δ from both right-hand sides changes the same dictionary to
x2​=10−Δ−x1​−2x3​−s1​,s2​=5−x1​−x3​+s1​,z=20−2Δ−x1​−3x3​−2s1​.
(29)
It remains feasible throughout 0≤Δ≤10, including the degenerate endpoint Δ=10, and the reduced coefficients are unchanged. Hence
zmax​(Δ)=20−2Δ,(x1​,x2​,x3​)=(0,10−Δ,0)​.
(30)
As an independent optimality certificate, z≤2(x1​+x2​+2x3​)≤2(10−Δ), with equality at the stated point. Negative reduced coefficients also prove uniqueness of the optimal decision vector.

In fact the right inverse gives the stronger splitting
U=kerα⊕W​.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
The Sylow theorems state that if a finite group has order ∣G∣=pam with p prime and p∤m, it has a subgroup of order pa, called a Sylow subgroup. Every p-group subgroup is contained in a Sylow subgroup, and all Sylow subgroups for the same prime are conjugate subgroups. Their number satisfies
np​≡1(modp),np​∣m​.
(33)
More precisely np​=[G:NG​(P)] for a Sylow subgroup P, where NG​(P) is its normalizer.

b

Words: 173 Articles: 1
10E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 173
b OurBigBook.com
A finite nonabelian simple group cannot be a p-group: a nontrivial finite p-group has nontrivial centre of a group, since its class equation makes every noncentral conjugacy class size divisible by p, and hence makes the centre size a positive multiple of p. That centre is a normal subgroup, so must be the whole group if G is a simple group, making it abelian; an abelian simple group has prime order. Therefore every Sylow subgroup here is nontrivial and proper. It cannot be normal, so np​>1.
To obtain a simple group embedding from Sylow conjugation, the conjugation action on Sylow subgroups gives a group homomorphism ρ:G→Snp​​. This group action is transitive by the Sylow theorems and is nontrivial since np​>1. Its kernel of a group homomorphism is a normal subgroup, so the defining property of a simple group makes the kernel of a group homomorphism trivial: ρ is an embedding. Now compose with the sign of a permutation Snp​​→{±1}. A nontrivial composite would again be injective because G is a simple group, embedding G in a group of order two, impossible for a nonabelian group. Thus ρ(G) lies in the alternating group Anp​​. By Lagrange's theorem,
∣G∣∣∣Anp​​∣=2np​!​​.
(34)
The argument only invokes the factorial formula once np​≥2; the impossible case np​=2 itself is also excluded by the embedding.

c OurBigBook.com
For order 48=24⋅3, the Sylow theorems give n2​∣3 and n2​≡1(mod2), hence n2​=1 or 3. If n2​=1, the Sylow subgroup of order 16 is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup. If G were simple in the other case, it would be nonabelian (a finite abelian simple group has prime order), and the preceding result would force 48∣3!/2=3, impossible. Thus every group of order 48 is not simple.
An example with no normal Sylow subgroup for p=2 is
G=S4​×C2​​.
(35)
In S4​, P=⟨(1234),(13)⟩ is a dihedral group of order 8: conjugation by (13) inverts (1234). Thus P×C2​ has order 16 and is a Sylow subgroup of G. The only transpositions in P are (13) and (24); conjugating (13) by (23) gives (12)∈/P. Therefore P and P×C2​ are not normal. By conjugacy, no other Sylow subgroup for p=2 is normal either.

i OurBigBook.com
A real function on a metric space is uniformly continuous if for every ε>0 there is a δ>0 such that, simultaneously for all x,y, d(x,y)<δ implies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<ε. For a continuous function on a finite closed interval [a,b], suppose this fails. Then there are ε0​>0 and pairs xn​,yn​ with ∣xn​−yn​∣<1/n but ∣f(xn​)−f(yn​)∣≥ε0​. By compactness, some subsequence xnj​​ converges to x∈[a,b]; then ynj​​→x too. Continuity contradicts the image separation. This proves the Heine-Cantor theorem in this setting. Boundedness of the interval matters: x2 on [0,∞) is a counterexample if “closed interval” includes unbounded intervals.
A function is Lipschitz continuous if some finite K≥0 satisfies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Kd(x,y) for every pair. Choosing δ=ε/(K+1) proves uniform continuity.
The first assertion is false. Take f(x)=sin(x2), which is bounded and continuous, and
xn​=2πn+π/2​,yn​=2πn+3π/2​.
(36)
Then f(xn​)=1, f(yn​)=−1, while yn​−xn​=π/(yn​+xn​)→0. This violates uniform continuity.

True. If ∣f′(x)∣≤K everywhere, the mean value theorem applied between any two distinct points gives
∣f(x)−f(y)∣=∣f′(ξ)∣∣x−y∣≤K∣x−y∣.
(37)
Thus f is Lipschitz continuous and hence uniformly continuous. No continuity of f′ is needed: differentiability of f gives continuity on each finite closed interval and is exactly the hypothesis needed for the mean value theorem there.

True. Define cn​(x)=max(−n,min(x,n)) and fn​=f∘cn​. The map cn​ is Lipschitz continuous with constant one. The restriction of f to [−n,n] is uniformly continuous by the Heine-Cantor theorem; its modulus of continuity combined with ∣cn​(x)−cn​(y)∣≤∣x−y∣ proves uniform continuity of fn​ on all of R. For each fixed x, once n≥∣x∣ we have fn​(x)=f(x). Hence
fn​⟶f pointwise on R​.
(38)
This pointwise approximation by uniformly continuous functions even gives eventual equality on every fixed bounded interval. It need not give uniform convergence on the whole line, as the bounded counterexample in part (i) already demonstrates.

If a nonempty subset S⊂R is not an interval, there are a,b∈S and c∈/S with a<c<b. The disjoint nonempty relatively open sets S∩(−∞,c) and S∩(c,∞) form a separation, so S is not connected.
Conversely, suppose an interval I had a separation into relatively open nonempty sets A,B. Choose a∈A,b∈B, interchanging the names if necessary so a<b. Put c=sup(A∩[a,b]). Because B contains a relative neighbourhood of b, c<b; because A contains a relative neighbourhood of a, c>a. Also c∈[a,b]⊂I. If c∈A, relative openness supplies points of A just above c, contradicting the supremum. If c∈B, a relative neighbourhood of c excludes points of A approaching c from below, again contradicting the supremum. Thus every interval is connected, including a singleton and unbounded or open intervals.
Take
K={0}∪{1/n:n≥1}​.
(39)
It is closed, because its only accumulation point is 0 and that point is included, and bounded. The Heine-Borel theorem makes it compact. The connected components of its complement are precisely
(−∞,0),(1,∞),(n+11​,n1​)(n≥1).
(40)
Each is an interval and therefore connected; none can be enlarged inside the complement across one of the intervening points of K.

Let a,b∈R2∖T. If a=b, use the constant path. Otherwise consider the countably many lines through a and a point of T, and through b and a point of T. Choose a line L whose direction is not parallel to any of these lines; such a direction exists because there are uncountably many directions but only a countable set of forbidden ones. Every forbidden line meets L in at most one point. Choose c∈L outside those countably many intersections and outside {a,b}.
Neither segment [a,c] nor [c,b] meets T: a forbidden point on either segment would put c on the corresponding forbidden line. The piecewise linear path
γ(t)={a+2t(c−a),c+(2t−1)(b−c),​0≤t≤1/2,1/2≤t≤1​
(41)
lies in the complement. This proves that the plane minus a countable set is path connected.
If a homeomorphism h:R2→R existed, its restriction after removing a point a would give a homeomorphism between R2∖{a} and R∖{h(a)}. The first is a path-connected space and therefore connected; the second consists of two separated intervals. Since homeomorphisms preserve connectedness, R2≅R​.

Fix Imλ>−c. Truncate C1​ at ±R−ic and close it with the upper semicircle centred at −ic, oriented counterclockwise. For large R the only pole of the integrand inside is z=λ. Uniformly on the arc, ∣z−λ∣ is comparable to R and f(z)=o(R−1), so the arc integral is o(R−1) and tends to zero. The line integral is absolutely convergent at infinity for the same decay reason. The Cauchy integral formula gives

The right-hand side is holomorphic on this open half-plane by the hypothesis, proving the required holomorphic function. The contour never passes through λ because its imaginary part is strictly above the line.

u(k)=(k2+1)(k2+q2)2​​=q2−12​(k2+11​−k2+q21​).

Both decay conditions hold. The first derivatives of the two exponential terms cancel at zero, so u is continuously differentiable there; the second derivatives have matching limits and the differential equation holds at zero as well as on both half-lines. For uniqueness, a difference solves the homogeneous equation. Decay gives Ae−qx on the positive half-line and Beqx on the negative half-line. Continuity gives A=B and derivative continuity gives −qA=qB, forcing both to be zero.
The PDF's condition ω=±1 also allows ω=0, but no decaying solution exists when ω=0. Indeed on x>0, −u′′=e−x and decay forces u=−e−x; on x<0, decay forces u=−ex. Their one-sided derivatives at zero are 1 and −1, which cannot match. The missing condition ω=0 is therefore a genuine source omission, not a transcription repair. The transform expression at q=0 has a nonintegrable k−2 singularity, consistently with this obstruction.

vtt​+k2v=0,v(k,0)=f​(k),vt​(k,0)=g​(k).
(51)
Solving this constant-coefficient ordinary differential equation gives
v(k,t)=f​(k)coskt+g​(k)ksinkt​​.

At k=0 the quotient means its continuous limit t, so v(0,t)=f​(0)+tg​(0).
Since coskt=(eikt+e−ikt)/2, the Translation property of the Fourier transform inverts the first term as (f(x+t)+f(x−t))/2. Also Kt​(x)=21​1[−t,t]​(x) has Fourier transform sinkt/k, including its limiting value at zero. The convolution theorem therefore inverts the second term as
(Kt​∗g)(x)=21​∫−tt​g(x−s)ds=21​∫x−tx+t​g(ξ)dξ.

This proves the D'Alembert formula
v(x,t)=2f(x−t)+f(x+t)​+21​∫x−tx+t​g(ξ)dξ​.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Define the parity operator by (Pψ)(x)=ψ(−x). For the usual full-line Hamiltonian operator, or any parity-invariant operator domain and boundary conditions, an even potential gives HP=PH: the second derivative is unchanged by reflection and V(−x)=V(x). If Hψ=Eψ, then H(Pψ)=E(Pψ). A nondegenerate energy eigenvalue has a one-dimensional eigenspace, so Pψ=σψ for some scalar σ. Since P2=I, σ2=1. Hence
Pψ=ψ or Pψ=−ψ​.
(55)
Thus the stationary state has even or odd parity. The symmetry must include the operator domain: an even potential alone would not imply this conclusion with asymmetric boundary conditions.

b

Solution

Words: 213
b OurBigBook.com
A bound state has E<0 and κ=−2mE​/ℏ>0, since outside the delta potentials a square-integrable solution must decay exponentially. The wavefunction is continuous at each delta: a jump would produce a delta derivative in ψ′′ with no matching term in the equation. Integrating the Time-independent Schrödinger equation across either x0​=±a gives
ψ(x0+​)=ψ(x0−​),ψ′(x0+​)−ψ′(x0−​)=−ℏ22mλ​ψ(x0​)​.
(56)
The symmetry of the symmetric double-delta potential permits even and odd solutions. Up to a nonzero normalization factor, the even candidate is cosh(κx) for ∣x∣≤a, and cosh(κa)e−κ(∣x∣−a) outside. Its derivative jump at a gives
κ(1+tanhκa)=ℏ22mλ​.
(57)
The odd candidate is sinh(κx) inside and sgn(x)sinh(κa)e−κ(∣x∣−a) outside. Its jump gives
κ(1+cothκa)=ℏ22mλ​.
(58)
Parity ensures the jump at −a as well. Put t=κa and L=2mλa/ℏ2. The continuous strictly increasing function t(1+tanht) ranges from 0 to infinity, so there is exactly one even bound state for every L>0. The continuous strictly increasing function t(1+cotht) ranges from 1 to infinity, so the odd bound state of a symmetric double-delta potential exists if and only if L>1. Strict increase follows from the allowed monotonicity facts plus the strictly increasing term t. Therefore
even: every λ>0;odd: λ>2maℏ2​​,E=−2mℏ2κ2​.
(59)
At equality the odd limiting solution has κ=0 and is not square integrable, so it is not a bound state. No nonnegative energy can supply another full-line square-integrable state, since its exterior solutions are oscillatory or affine.

In a source-free vacuum, Maxwell equations are
∇⋅E=0,∇⋅B=0,∇×E=−∂t​B,∇×B=μ0​ϵ0​∂t​E.
(60)
Taking a curl of the last two equations and using ∇×(∇×A)=∇(∇⋅A)−∇2A gives the electromagnetic wave equations
Ett​=c2∇2E,Btt​=c2∇2B,c=μ0​ϵ0​​1​​.
(61)
Substitution of the complex plane wave amplitudes into Maxwell equations, then taking real parts, gives
k⋅e=k⋅b=0,k×e=ωb,k×b=−c2ω​e.
(62)
For a nonzero propagating wave these imply the dispersion relation ω2=c2∣k∣2​. Conversely choose any nonzero transverse complex e and set b=k×e/ω to obtain such a wave. The static uniform-field sector at ω=∣k∣=0 is separate from propagation.
At a perfect conductor, the oscillatory boundary conditions are n×E=0 and n⋅B=0. Surface charge and surface current allow nonzero normal electric and tangential magnetic fields. The magnetic condition here concerns the time-dependent wave field; a perfect conductor can retain a pre-existing static magnetic field.
Let R=I−2nnT be the orthogonal reflection across the boundary plane, so detR=−1. The proposed reflected amplitudes are k′=Rk, e′=−Re, and b′=Rb. For an orthogonal reflection, (Ra)×(Rd)=−R(a×d). Hence
k′×e′=ωb′,k′×b′=−c2ω​e′,k′⋅e′=k′⋅b′=0.
(63)
Also ∣k′∣=∣k∣, so the reflected wave obeys the same dispersion relation. At n⋅x=0, the incident and reflected phases coincide because k′−k is parallel to n. Their summed amplitudes satisfy
e+e′=2(n⋅e)n,b+b′=2[b−(n⋅b)n].
(64)
The first has zero tangential part and the second zero normal part, proving both boundary conditions. Finally k′⋅n=−k⋅n>0, as required for reflection into the vacuum.

Choose x downslope along the rigid plane and z normal to it into the fluid, with the wall at z=0 and the flat free surface at z=h. The gravitational body force per unit volume has components (ρgsinα,−ρgcosα). The wind's tangential traction on the top surface is −S in the x direction; the atmospheric normal traction is −patm​ in the z direction. At the wall there is no-slip boundary condition, and the wall supplies the opposing normal force and a tangential traction whose sign depends on the wind strength.
The velocity is parallel to the plane, (u(z),0). Its velocity profile is a concave quadratic, with u(0)=0 and negative slope at the free surface when S>0. The diagram uses moderate wind, for which the flow is still everywhere downslope. Stronger wind can reverse the upper portion, or the entire moving layer; the later cases quantify this.

For an inclined viscous film with opposing surface shear, the steady parallel velocity automatically satisfies the continuity equation and the advective acceleration vanishes. The two components of the Navier-Stokes equations reduce to
0=−px​+μu′′+ρgsinα,0=−pz​−ρgcosα.
(65)
The uniform thickness and constant atmospheric pressure make px​=0. The boundary conditions are
u(0)=0,μu′(h)=−S,p(h)=patm​.
(66)
These are respectively no-slip boundary condition, imposed tangential traction on the surface with outward normal +ez​, and the normal stress condition on the flat free surface. The normal viscous stress is zero because the normal velocity vanishes. Integrating gives
u(z)=μρgsinα​(hz−2z2​)−μS​z,p(z)=patm​+ρgcosα(h−z)​.

In particular μu′(0)=ρghsinα−S is the downslope tangential traction exerted by the fluid on the wall. The wall's tangential traction on the fluid has the opposite sign, because the outward normal of the fluid at its bottom is −ez​. This fixes the potentially confusing wall sign convention.

k2​k3​​=f+ha1​f′f+21​h2a12​f′′[f,f]+O(h3),=f+h(a2​+a3​)f′f+h2(a1​a3​(f′)2f+21​(a2​+a3​)2f′′[f,f])+O(h3).​

The exact flow has Taylor expansion

Matching the terms through h3 in the Runge-Kutta method gives the sufficient third-order conditions for an explicit Runge-Kutta method

Words: 163 Articles: 1
19H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 163
a OurBigBook.com
A sufficient statistic has a conditional distribution of the full data given its value that is independent of the unknown parameter. A minimal sufficient statistic is sufficient and is a function of every other sufficient statistic, up to null sets. For a dominated family with common positive support, the likelihood-ratio criterion for minimal sufficiency states that T is minimal sufficient if T(x)=T(y) holds exactly when pθ​(x)/pθ​(y) is independent of θ.
For S=∑i​Xi​, the joint probability mass function is
pθ​(x)=θ−n(1−1/θ)S−n,xi​≥1.
(75)
The Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem proves sufficiency of S. For two samples, the likelihood ratio is (1−1/θ)S(x)−S(y), independent of θ>1 exactly when their sums agree. Thus S is minimal sufficient. Any one-to-one transformation of it is also minimal sufficient, so choose
T=X=nS​,Eθ​T=θ​.
(76)
This chosen estimator is an unbiased estimator, since each observation has mean θ. If instead the statistic is reported as S, its expectation is nθ, and as an estimator of θ it has bias (n−1)θ (zero only when n=1). Being a minimal sufficient statistic is unchanged by this rescaling; being an unbiased estimator is not.

For a target a(θ), the bias of an integrable estimator T is Eθ​T−a(θ); it is an unbiased estimator if this is zero at every allowed parameter value. Here Y has a zero-truncated Poisson distribution, θ>0, and p=1−e−θ∈(0,1). Write an estimator based only on Y as t(Y), assuming a finite expectation for every θ>0. Unbiasedness requires
∑y=1∞​t(y)y!θy​=(eθ−1)(1−e−θ)=eθ+e−θ−2.
(77)
Absolute integrability at every positive parameter ensures that the power series on the left converges absolutely on every complex disc. Uniqueness of coefficients in a power series therefore gives t(y)=0 for odd y and t(y)=2 for positive even y. Conversely these values give the displayed identity, so
T=21{Y even}​​
(78)
is the unique unbiased estimator of this form. The uniqueness claim concerns nonrandomized functions of Y; allowing external randomness would permit addition of independent mean-zero noise.
For this parity estimator for a zero-truncated Poisson count, usefulness depends on the loss, but under squared-error loss it performs poorly despite being an unbiased estimator. Since P(Y even)=p/2, ET2=2p and
VarT=2p−p2=1−e−2θ.
(79)
It takes the inadmissible value 2 with positive probability, and its variance tends to one rather than zero as θ→∞. Clipping to the parameter interval gives Tc​=min(T,1)=1{Y even}​. This has bias −p/2, but
E[(Tc​−p)2]=p/2<2p−p2=E[(T−p)2],0<p<1.
(80)
Thus a simple biased estimator strictly improves its mean squared error at every parameter value; uniqueness among unbiased estimators does not make it optimal for this loss.

Solution

Assume the intended initial fortune satisfies n≥2 and put X0​=n. Conditional on current fortune i>1, the next gift is uniform on {1,…,i−1} and independent of the previous choices. The remaining fortune is therefore uniform on that same set. At fortune 1 the process stays there. Consequently the future conditional distribution depends only on the current fortune, proving the Markov property, and the transition matrix on {1,…,n} is
Pij​=⎩⎨⎧​1,1/(i−1),0,​i=j=1,i>1, 1≤j<i,otherwise.​​
(81)
The uniform decreasing Markov chain has state 1 as an absorbing state, and until absorption the fortune strictly decreases, so the hitting time is at most n−1.
Let ei​ be the expected number of additional transitions to hit 1, taking e1​=0. First-step analysis gives
ei​=1+i−11​∑j=1i−1​ej​(i≥2).
(82)
In particular e2​=1. For i≥3, multiplying this recurrence by i−1 and the recurrence for i−1 by i−2, then subtracting, gives (i−1)ei​=(i−1)ei−1​+1. Hence ei​−ei−1​=1/(i−1) for every i≥2, and telescoping yields
En​τ=en​=j=1∑n−1​j1​=Hn−1​​.
(83)
The PDF defines τ using times i≥1. If n=1 were included, that definition would give τ=1 although the displayed empty sum is zero; the initial instruction to choose an integer between 1 and n−1 also requires n≥2. The result above uses that intended assumption. A hitting time allowing time zero would have expectation zero from state 1, but that is a different definition.
